assetEditor.animatedError: This image is animated, so it can't be edited—editing would flatten it to a single frame.
assetEditor.applyNote: The edit goes back into the generation history at {{width}}×{{height}}. Nothing reaches the asset library until you save it there.
assetEditor.clashesWithOther: Another asset is already called “{{name}}”. Saving makes a second one with that name, and “bg: {{name}}” in a scene could then mean either of them.
assetEditor.clashesWithSelf: That is the name of the asset you are editing. “Save as new” would give you two assets called “{{name}}”, and “bg: {{name}}” in a scene could mean either—use “Overwrite Original” instead.
assetEditor.cpuEngineNote: Runs on your machine—no image is uploaded. First use downloads {{name}} (about {{size}}, {{license}}) and keeps it. It reasons at {{resolution}} pixels, then the edge is refined against your full-size image. The second, closer pass is skipped on the CPU; the result is a little coarser and takes half as long.
assetEditor.cpuSlowNote: Nothing is stuck. The CPU runs the whole model one layer at a time, and the percentage is a guess from how long this machine took last time—it can finish early or run over.
assetEditor.cpuWarning: Running on your CPU, not a graphics card. One image takes roughly a minute instead of a second, the browser tab stays busy the whole time, and the first use downloads {{size}} of weights. {{reason}}
assetEditor.cropHint: Drag across the image to crop it. Click once to start over.
assetEditor.engineNote: Runs on your machine, on {{gpu}}—no image is uploaded. First use downloads {{name}} (about {{size}}, {{license}}) and keeps it, so later cutouts start straight away. It reasons at {{resolution}} pixels, then the edge is refined against your full-size image.
assetEditor.name: Name
assetEditor.needsRealGpu: Your browser is running WebGPU on a software renderer (SwiftShader), not on your graphics card. Turn on “Use graphics acceleration when available” in your browser settings, and if it is already on, check chrome://gpu to see why your card was rejected.
assetEditor.needsWebGpu: Removing the background needs WebGPU, which this browser doesn't have. Try a recent Chrome or Edge.
assetEditor.onCpuError: One pass took {{seconds}} seconds, which means the model is running on your CPU rather than your graphics card—it would take many minutes and the result would be no better. Your browser reports its GPU as: {{gpu}}. Check that hardware acceleration is on in your browser settings, then reload.
assetEditor.replacePrompt: Overwrite “{{name}}” with this edit? Every scene using it will show the new version. The original pixels are gone for good—this cannot be undone.
assetEditor.saveError: Could not save the edited asset.
assetEditor.saveNote: “Save as new” makes a separate {{width}}×{{height}} asset and leaves the original alone. “Overwrite” replaces it in place, keeping its name so scenes already using it follow along. Either way the edits are baked into the pixels.
assetEditor.slowNote: The first cutout is the slow one: your GPU has to compile the model, and it runs twice. Later ones take a second or two.

assetEditor.tuningNote: Drag these if too much or too little was cut—they re-use the cutout the model already made, so they apply instantly. Lower “keep ↔ cut” rescues a subject that came out full of holes; higher softness keeps the model’s own soft edges instead of forcing them to solid or clear.

welcome.autosave:
There's now a folder named Twine in your Documents folder. Inside that is a Stories folder, where all your work will be saved. Twine saves as you work, so you don't have to worry about remembering to save it yourself. You can always open the folder your stories are saved to by using the Show Library item in the Twine menu.

Because Twine is always saving your work, the files in your story library will be locked from editing while Twine is open.

If you'd like to open a Twine story file you received from someone else, you can import it into your library using the Import From File link in the story list.
welcome.browserStorage:
That means you don't need to create an account to use Twine 2, and everything you create isn't stored on a server somewhere else—it stays right in your browser.

Two very important things to remember, though. Since your work is saved only in your browser, if you clear its saved data, then you'll lose your work! Not good. Remember to use that Archive button often. You can also publish individual stories to files using the menu on each story in the story list. Both archive and story files can always be re-imported into Twine.

Secondly, anyone who can use this browser can see and make changes to your work. So if you've got a nosy kid brother, look into setting up a separate profile for yourself.
welcome.browserStorageTitle: Your work is only saved in your browser
welcome.done: Thanks for reading, and have fun with Twine.
welcome.greeting: Twine is an open-source tool for telling interactive, nonlinear stories. There are a few things you should know before you get started.
welcome.help: If you've never used Twine before, then welcome! The Twine Cookbook is a great resource for learning how to use it. If you haven't used Twine before, it's a great place to start.
